Rehum
rē'hum
n. (the Persian chancellor whose letter halted the rebuilding of Jerusalem; also a Levite who repaired the wall under Nehemiah)
From Hebrew Rechum, connected with racham, to have compassion — “compassionate”. The chancellor of Ezra 4 bore a merciful name and wrote a merciless letter.

Biblical Definition

Rehum the chancellor is the official who stopped the work at Jerusalem for the better part of a generation. When the adversaries of Judah were refused a share in building the temple, they turned to the imperial post: “Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king” (Ezr 4:8). The letter is a model of its kind — professed loyalty to the crown, an appeal to the archives, and a warning that this rebellious and bad city, once rebuilt, would pay no toll, tribute or custom. The king searched the records, found that Jerusalem had indeed made insurrection of old, and ordered the work stopped. “Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power” (Ezr 4:23). The haste is the detail that gives them away. A second and very different Rehum appears in Nehemiah's day, a Levite with a trowel: “After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani” (Neh 3:17), and a Rehum seals the covenant of Nehemiah 10. The same name serves the opposition and the rebuilding, which is how it usually goes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Rehum; in sacred history the name belongs to the Persian chancellor who wrote against Jerusalem, and to a Levite who repaired the wall.

expand to see more

REHUM, n. The name signifies compassionate or merciful.

Rehum the chancellor wrote to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem.

By his letter the work of the house of God ceased until the second year of Darius.

A Levite of the same name, the son of Bani, repaired a portion of the wall under Nehemiah.

Others of the name are found among those who returned with Zerubbabel and sealed the covenant.

Key Scripture

Ezr 4:8 — "Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort:"

Ezr 4:23 — "Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power."

Neh 3:17 — "After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani. Next unto him repaired Hashabiah, the ruler of the half part of Keilah, in his part."

Ezr 3:2 — "Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses the man of God."

Modern Corruption

Opposition to the work of God is expected to come as open persecution; Ezra 4 shows it arriving as paperwork, legality and concern for public order, which is far commoner and harder to answer.

expand to see more

The adversaries in Ezra 4 begin by asking to help build. Refused, they hire counsellors, weaken the hands of the people, and finally write a letter that is accurate in most of its particulars and devastating in its effect. Nobody in the story breaks a law. The opposition is procedural, respectable and successful, and it costs the temple sixteen years. The church has generally braced for the lion and been undone by the clerk. Scripture's counsel for such seasons is not a technique but a posture: the elders of the Jews kept building when the word of God came by Haggai and Zechariah, and answered the next enquiry by telling the plain truth about who they were and whose house it was (Ezr 5:11).

There is a second lesson in the two Rehums. One used an office to stop the work; the other took a section of broken wall and repaired it. Nehemiah 3 is a chapter of names doing exactly that — goldsmiths, apothecaries, rulers of districts, a man and his daughters — and the wall went up in fifty-two days because a great many people each mended what was in front of them. The New Testament has the same architecture: the body “maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love” when “every joint supplieth” and every part works in its measure (Eph 4:16). Chancellors get letters into the archives. Levites with trowels get walls built.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Rechum (H7348), Rehum; racham (H7355), to have compassion; be'el te'em, chancellor, lord of decree; saphar (H5608), scribe; batel, to cease, be made to stop.

expand to see more

Hebrew Rechum (H7348) — Rehum; the name means compassionate.

Hebrew racham (H7355) — to love deeply, have mercy; the root of the name.

Aramaic be'el te'em — lord of the decree, rendered “chancellor”; his office under Persia.

Hebrew saphar (H5608) — to write, to be a scribe; Shimshai's office beside him.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, repair; the verb of Nehemiah 3, used of the other Rehum.

Usage

"“Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem” — opposition with a filing number."

"“They went up in haste… and made them to cease by force and power” — the eagerness gives the motive away."

"“After him repaired the Levites, Rehum the son of Bani” — the same name, the other side of the wall."
